questions.q: Define "secondary theme" in your own words and give one example from any story you have read previously (not from this play).
questions.a: A secondary theme is a recurring idea that supports or contrasts with the main theme but is not the central focus; for example, in "The Necklace" by Maupassant, the primary theme is the danger of vanity, while a secondary theme is the cruelty of social class distinctions. A wrong answer that merely repeats the primary theme definition or gives a plot event instead of a thematic idea reveals the student cannot distinguish between theme hierarchy levels.

questions.q: In the play, the mother (yhyk) says: "मैं तो यही कहती हूँ कि वकील साहब को ट्यूशन करना ही पड़ेगा... बच्चों के भविष्य का सवाल है।" Explain what secondary theme this dialogue reveals and why it is not the primary theme.
questions.a: This dialogue reveals the secondary theme of "parental pragmatism vs. systemic exploitation" — the mother accepts the corrupt tuition system as unavoidable for her child's survival. It is not the primary theme because the play's central critique targets the tuition culture itself, not the mother's compromise. A wrong answer that labels this as the primary theme shows the student conflates a character's coping strategy with the author's central argument.

questions.q: Identify one stage direction from the text that conveys economic disparity without any character speaking about money directly. Quote the stage direction and explain its thematic function.
questions.a: Stage direction: "निम्न मध्यम वर्ग के एक छोटे से मकान का एक दृश्य... एक टूटी हुई कुर्सी... दीवार पर टंगी हुई एक पुरानी तस्वीर।" This visual description establishes the family's poverty as a constant backdrop, making their desperate acceptance of tuition fees thematically inevitable rather than a mere choice. A wrong answer that quotes a spoken line about fees instead of a silent visual detail shows the student cannot distinguish thematic encoding in stagecraft from dialogue.

questions.q: Compare the father (जतüh) and the teacher (गृहलक्ष्मी) in their responses to the tuition system. How do their contrasting stances create a secondary theme about "complicity of the educated"?
questions.a: The father opposes tuition verbally but ultimately sends the child; the teacher refuses to give tuition personally but upholds school rules that make tuition necessary. Together they illustrate that even well-meaning educated individuals become complicit in systemic corruption through inaction or institutional obedience. A wrong answer that treats them as simply "good vs. bad" characters misses the thematic nuance that both are trapped in the same structure.

questions.q: Critique the view that the play's secondary theme of "gendered division of labor" is merely a background detail. Use two specific scenes to defend your position.
questions.a: The gendered division of labor is structurally essential: Scene 1 shows the mother managing household finances and tuition negotiations while the father debates principles; Scene 3 shows the mother physically feeding the child during the tuition discussion, symbolizing her role as the nurturer who bears the practical burden. Removing this theme would collapse the play's realism about how systemic pressures fall disproportionately on women. A wrong answer that calls it "just setting" reveals inability to see how character roles enact thematic arguments.

questions.q: Write a 4-line poetic stanza that captures the secondary theme of "the child's silenced voice" using imagery from the play (e.g., broken chair, certificate, tuition fee receipt).
questions.a:
टूटी कुर्सी पर बैठा डर,
सर्टिफिकेट की आस लिए,
फीस की रसीद नहीं बोलती,
बच्चे की चुप्पी ही गवाह बने।
A poor answer that describes the plot instead of evoking the theme through imagery shows the student cannot transform thematic analysis into creative synthesis.
